vignette:
Anna Keller is a 40-year-old married data scientist who came to treatment after several years of trying to contain her life by tightening it around work. The event she returns to began while she was traveling in a region marked by longstanding ethnic tension. She had gone through an area near Arab villages during a period when the atmosphere already felt strained and watchful. What she witnessed was an attack involving fire. She remembers the flames first as something unreal in their brightness and speed, then the sounds—shouting, panic, the sharp, confused noise of people reacting all at once. In the moment, her attention fixed on other people who were exposed and vulnerable. Since then, what has stayed with her most forcefully is the conviction that she should have done something to protect them. She says this not as an abstract regret but as a settled judgment about herself: she failed, and someone better, stronger, or quicker would not have been in that position or would have acted differently.

In the weeks afterward, Anna found that the memory did not behave like an ordinary recollection. She could be moving through a normal day and, without warning, something in her surroundings would bring the whole scene back. The memory arrived with such force that it felt more real than the rest of the room she was standing in. At times she did not simply picture the event; she heard it again in her head, the same sounds from that day cutting through the present. During these episodes she could suddenly feel as if she were back there rather than in her kitchen, her office, or a grocery store aisle. A glimpse of open flame at a restaurant table, a fire pit in a neighbor’s yard, even a brief view of flames on a television screen could seize her body before she had time to think. News images or passing references connected to Arab villages also had a peculiar immediacy for her, not as political topics but as portals into the exact setting in which the event took place.

As time went on, Anna began organizing her life around staying mentally occupied. She works in a demanding data science role and discovered that dense analytical tasks, long coding sessions, and late-night problem solving gave her temporary relief because they left little room for the memory to break through. She started taking on extra projects and stretching her workdays well past what was required. Her colleagues praised her productivity, but at home her husband saw that she was using work to avoid the unstructured parts of evening when she might be alone with her thoughts. Even when she stopped working, her mind did not rest. She would go over and over why the event had happened to her, why she had been there, and what exact moment she should have acted differently. The thinking felt compulsory, as if there might be some final answer that would either explain her failure or undo it.

Her sense of danger also changed in ordinary settings. Strangers approaching her on the street, in a parking garage, or even in the lobby outside her office could feel threatening before they had done anything at all. She noticed herself tracking people’s movements and tensing when someone came too close. At home she began checking doors and windows repeatedly at night. She knew on one level that the neighborhood was not the site of the trauma, but the checking still felt necessary, as if failing to do it would leave her responsible again for whatever might happen next. Stress made everything worse. During high-pressure periods at work, especially before deadlines, she was more likely to be hit by vivid re-experiencing and more likely to patrol the house before bed. Her husband initially tried to reassure her, then became frustrated by how long the checking could last and by how often she retreated back to her laptop afterward.

What finally brought Anna to seek help was not one single crisis but a narrowing of her life she could no longer dismiss. She had become someone who felt unsafe around ordinary people, who could be pulled out of the present by the sight of flame, and who measured herself constantly against an imagined other person who would have protected everyone. In her lowest moments she has found herself thinking she is not sure her life is worth living anymore, less as a wish to die than as a bleak verdict on who she has become since the event. Coming to treatment, she says she wants relief from the sudden vividness of the memory and from the relentless judgment that follows it. What frightens her most is the possibility that this is permanent—that she will remain forever the person who stood there and failed.
